section-4: Historians use 'early modern' for roughly 1500-1800 to describe changes shared across Eurasia: large gunpowder empires (the Mughals, Safavids and Ottomans), expanding global trade after the European voyages, the circulation of American silver and new crops, growing commercialisation, bureaucratic states and new forms of religious and cultural expression. The term avoids the older colonial division of Indian history into 'Hindu', 'Muslim' and 'British' periods.

In India, this period covers the Mughal empire (1526-1857, effectively until the early eighteenth century), the Deccan Sultanates and Vijayanagara, the rise of regional states such as the Marathas, Sikhs, Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad, and the growing presence of European trading companies. It ends with the transition to colonial rule in the late eighteenth century.
section-5: At the beginning of the sixteenth century, the Delhi Sultanate under the Lodis (Ibrahim Lodi, 1517-1526) controlled only part of north India, and Afghan nobles were discontented. Independent kingdoms included Gujarat, Malwa, Bengal, Jaunpur and Kashmir; the Rajput confederacy under Rana Sanga of Mewar was powerful; in the south were Vijayanagara under Krishnadevaraya and the Bahmani successor states; and the Portuguese controlled Goa and parts of the western coast.

Daulat Khan Lodi, governor of Punjab, and Alam Khan, Ibrahim's uncle, invited Babur to invade, hoping to use him against Ibrahim. The political division of north India made it possible for Babur, with a small but well-equipped army, to establish his rule.
section-6: Babur (Zahiruddin Muhammad, 1483-1530) was descended from Timur on his father's side and Chinggis Khan on his mother's. He lost his kingdom of Ferghana in Central Asia, captured Kabul (1504) and turned towards India. At the First Battle of Panipat (21 April 1526), he defeated Ibrahim Lodi using the tulughma tactic (flanking attacks by cavalry), artillery (managed by Ustad Ali and Mustafa) and the 'Ottoman device' (araba) of carts tied together to protect gunners.

He then defeated Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527), declaring a jihad to motivate his troops, Medini Rai at Chanderi (1528), and the Afghans at Ghaghra (1529). He wrote his memoirs, the 'Baburnama' (Tuzuk-i-Baburi), in Chaghatai Turkish, describing India's people, plants and animals. He died in 1530. His son Humayun lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri (battles of Chausa 1539 and Kannauj 1540), and recovered it only in 1555.
section-7: Akbar (1556-1605) became emperor at thirteen. Under his guardian Bairam Khan he defeated Hemu at the Second Battle of Panipat (1556). He conquered Malwa, Gujarat (1572-1573), Bengal and Bihar (1574-1576), Kashmir, Sindh, Kandahar and parts of the Deccan (Ahmadnagar, Khandesh). His Rajput policy combined conquest (Chittor 1568, Ranthambhor) with marriage alliances (with the Kachhwaha princess of Amber, Harkha Bai) and high positions for Rajput nobles such as Raja Man Singh. Rana Pratap of Mewar resisted (Battle of Haldighati, 1576).

Administratively, he introduced the mansabdari system (ranks of zat and sawar), the zabt revenue system of Todar Mal, the division of the empire into subas (provinces) with uniform officials (subadar, diwan, bakhshi, sadr, qazi, kotwal), and the jagir system. His policy of sulh-i-kul (universal peace) and abolition of the jizya (1564) and pilgrim tax won the loyalty of non-Muslims.
section-8: At the top were the emperor, the royal family and the nobility (umara) - a mixed group of Turanis (Central Asians), Iranis, Afghans, Indian Muslims (Shaikhzadas), Rajputs and later Marathas, ranked as mansabdars. The ulema (Muslim scholars) and Hindu Brahmanas formed religious elites. Zamindars, ranging from powerful chiefs to small landholders, controlled local power and collected revenue.

Merchants and bankers (such as the Jain banker Virji Vora of Surat), artisans in towns (weavers, metalworkers) and the peasants (raiyat), divided into khud-kashta (resident cultivators) and pahi-kashta (non-resident or migrant cultivators), formed the bulk of society. Caste and jati shaped rural life. Women of the elite lived in purdah but some, like Nur Jahan and Jahanara, wielded political and economic influence. Foreign travellers such as Bernier and Manucci described great inequality between the rich and the poor.
section-9: Architecture: Humayun's Tomb in Delhi (1560s, built by his widow Hamida Banu Begum and designed by Mirak Mirza Ghiyas) introduced the char bagh garden and double dome. Akbar built Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri (with the Buland Darwaza, Diwan-i-Khas, Panch Mahal, Jodha Bai's palace) combining Persian and Indian styles in red sandstone. Jahangir built the tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah (pietra dura inlay in marble). Shah Jahan, the greatest builder, created the Taj Mahal (1632-1653, for Mumtaz Mahal), the Red Fort and Jama Masjid in Delhi (Shahjahanabad) and the Peacock Throne. Aurangzeb built the Badshahi Mosque in Lahore and Bibi ka Maqbara in Aurangabad.

Painting: Humayun brought Persian painters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad. Akbar's atelier illustrated the Hamzanama, Akbarnama and Persian translations of the Mahabharata (Razmnama); painters included Daswanth and Basawan. Under Jahangir, Mughal painting reached its height with portraits and nature studies (Ustad Mansur's birds and animals, Abul Hasan). European influence introduced perspective and haloes. Music also flourished (Tansen at Akbar's court).
section-10: Persian was the court language. Major historical works include Abul Fazl's 'Akbarnama' and 'Ain-i-Akbari' (a detailed statistical account of Akbar's empire), Badauni's critical 'Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh', Nizamuddin Ahmad's 'Tabaqat-i-Akbari', Jahangir's memoir 'Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri', Abdul Hamid Lahori's 'Padshahnama' and Gulbadan Begum's 'Humayun-nama'. Dara Shikoh translated the Upanishads into Persian ('Sirr-i-Akbar') and wrote 'Majma-ul-Bahrain' on the confluence of Islam and Hinduism.

Literature in other languages flourished: Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas), Surdas, Rahim and Raskhan in Hindi; Faizi translated Sanskrit works; Urdu poetry developed later (Wali Dakhani, Mir, Ghalib). In science, Akbar was interested in technology and Jai Singh II of Amber later built observatories (Jantar Mantar at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi). Mughal agriculture and medicine also saw developments, though India did not undergo a scientific revolution like Europe.
section-11: Babur and Humayun followed Sunni Islam but were practical. Akbar's policy evolved: he abolished the pilgrim tax (1563) and jizya (1564), built the Ibadat Khana (1575) at Fatehpur Sikri for religious debates among Sunni and Shia scholars, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuits, issued the Mahzar (1579) declaring himself the final arbiter on religious matters, and founded the Din-i-Ilahi (Tauhid-i-Ilahi, 1582), a spiritual discipleship rather than a new religion. His ideal was sulh-i-kul (peace with all).

Jahangir and Shah Jahan largely continued this tolerance but with greater Islamic orthodoxy under Shah Jahan. Aurangzeb (1658-1707) adopted a more orthodox policy: he banned music at court, destroyed some temples (such as Kashi Vishwanath and Keshava Rai at Mathura), reimposed jizya (1679), and executed the Sikh Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675). Historians debate the extent to which his policies were driven by religion or political considerations; he also gave grants to some temples and employed many Hindu nobles.
section-12: The 'jagirdari crisis' (Satish Chandra) arose because the number of mansabdars increased faster than the available land for jagirs (be-jagiri), especially under Aurangzeb, when many Deccani and Maratha nobles were admitted. Jagirdars, frequently transferred, oppressed peasants to extract maximum revenue, leading to peasant revolts. Long, expensive wars in the Deccan (1681-1707) drained the treasury.

After Aurangzeb, wars of succession, weak emperors (the 'puppet' emperors controlled by the Sayyid brothers), factional conflict among Turani, Irani and Hindustani nobles and invasions by Nadir Shah of Persia (1739, who sacked Delhi and took the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor) and Ahmad Shah Abdali (several times from 1748, defeating the Marathas at Panipat in 1761) weakened the empire. Provincial governors became independent in Hyderabad (Nizam-ul-Mulk, 1724), Bengal (Murshid Quli Khan) and Awadh (Saadat Khan).
section-13: Marathas: Shivaji (1630-1680) built an independent kingdom in western Maharashtra, using forts and guerrilla warfare against Bijapur and the Mughals, and was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674. He had a council of eight ministers (Ashtapradhan) and collected chauth (one-fourth) and sardeshmukhi (an additional tenth) from neighbouring territories. After his son Sambhaji was executed by Aurangzeb (1689), the Marathas continued resistance. In the eighteenth century the Peshwas (Balaji Vishwanath, Baji Rao I) expanded Maratha power across India until the defeat at Panipat (1761).

Sikhs: Guru Nanak (1469-1539) founded Sikhism; Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth and was executed by Jahangir (1606); Guru Hargobind militarised the community; Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa (1699). After his death, Banda Bahadur led a peasant revolt (executed 1716). In the eighteenth century, Sikh misls (confederacies) controlled Punjab, and Ranjit Singh united them into a kingdom (capturing Lahore, 1799).
section-14: The Mughal army was based on cavalry provided by mansabdars, supplemented by the emperor's own troops (ahadis), infantry, artillery and war elephants. Firearms - cannons, matchlock muskets (banduq) - became important from Babur's time, though cavalry remained central. Forts (Agra, Gwalior, Chittor, the Deccan forts) were key to controlling territory and were taken by long sieges.

Jos Gommans ('Mughal Warfare') argued that war in India involved negotiation, bribery and alliances as much as battles, and that the 'military labour market' allowed rulers to hire soldiers from peasant communities. Military finance depended on land revenue. In the eighteenth century, European-style trained infantry and artillery, adopted by the Marathas, Mysore (Tipu Sultan's rockets) and the Sikhs, as well as by the English East India Company, changed warfare.
section-15: In the early modern period, the Indian Ocean was a busy trading zone. Gujarati ports (Surat, Cambay), Malabar (Calicut, Cochin), Coromandel (Masulipatnam, Pulicat) and Bengal (Hooghly, Chittagong) traded with the Red Sea, the Persian Gulf, East Africa, Southeast Asia and China. India exported textiles (cotton cloth was the most important commodity), indigo, saltpetre, pepper, sugar and grain, and imported silver, gold, horses, spices and luxury goods.

Indian merchants such as the Gujarati banias and Bohras, Chettis of Coromandel and Mappilas of Malabar were active; the Surat merchant Abdul Ghafur owned a fleet comparable to the whole English East India Company's. The Portuguese tried to control trade through cartazes; the Dutch (VOC, 1602) and English (EIC, 1600) East India Companies later established factories. Historians such as Ashin Das Gupta and K. N. Chaudhuri studied this trade.
section-16: From 1500 to 1650, South India was dominated by Vijayanagara (until 1565) and its successors - the Nayakas of Madurai, Thanjavur and Gingee, and the Aravidu rulers at Chandragiri - and by the Deccan Sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda. The nayaka system gave military chiefs control over territories in return for service and payments, which led to the emergence of autonomous Nayaka kingdoms after 1565.

The economy linked agriculture (rice in the river deltas, tank irrigation), temple institutions, weaving and trade. The Coromandel coast exported large quantities of cotton textiles to Southeast Asia and later to Europe, through ports such as Pulicat (Dutch) and Madras (founded by the English in 1639). Merchant groups such as the Chettis and Komatis financed both trade and states. Sanjay Subrahmanyam's 'The Political Economy of Commerce: Southern India 1500-1650' examines these links between politics, agrarian systems and commerce.
section-17: Administrative legacy: the zabt land revenue system, divisions such as subas, sarkars and parganas, the mansabdari system and terms such as diwan, kotwal and qanungo influenced British administration. The British retained Persian as the court language until 1837 and continued many Mughal revenue practices.

Cultural legacy: Indo-Islamic architecture (the Taj Mahal, Red Fort), Mughal and Rajput painting, Hindustani music, the Urdu language, Mughlai cuisine (biryani, kebabs, kormas), garden design, dress (the jama, the angarkha), courtly etiquette and the composite culture of Hindustan (sometimes called Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb). The idea of a united empire over most of India also influenced later ideas of India as a political unit.
section-19: Pre-Mughal background: north India was divided among the Lodis, Rajputs (Rana Sanga) and regional sultanates; Vijayanagara and the Bahmani successor states ruled the south. Babur's victories at Panipat (1526), Khanwa (1527) and Ghaghra (1529), using artillery and cavalry tactics, established Mughal rule. Humayun lost the empire to the Afghan Sher Shah Suri (1540-1545), whose reforms - land measurement, the rupiya silver coin, the Grand Trunk Road and sarais - were later continued by Akbar. Humayun regained Delhi in 1555.

Akbar's consolidation: conquests extended the empire from Kabul to Bengal and Gujarat to the Deccan. His Rajput policy - marriage alliances, high mansabs and autonomy (watan jagirs) for loyal chiefs - turned enemies into partners. He created a centralised administration through the mansabdari system (each officer ranked by zat, personal rank, and sawar, cavalry obligation), the jagir system (assignments of revenue), and the zabt system (measurement and fixed cash revenue based on average produce). Provinces (subas) had uniform officials whose powers checked each other.

Ideology: Akbar's religious tolerance, sulh-i-kul, the Ibadat Khana debates, the Mahzar and the Din-i-Ilahi, along with the abolition of jizya, created loyalty among diverse subjects. Abul Fazl presented the emperor as a divinely illuminated ruler (farr-i-izadi). His successors Jahangir (1605-1627) and Shah Jahan (1628-1658) expanded the empire into the Deccan, while Aurangzeb (1658-1707) brought it to its maximum extent. The Mughal empire was therefore both a conquest state and a carefully constructed system of alliances, administration and ideology.
section-20: Society: the ruling elite of emperor and mansabdars was ethnically and religiously mixed; zamindars controlled local society; merchants, bankers and artisans flourished in towns such as Agra, Delhi, Lahore, Surat, Ahmedabad and Dhaka; and peasants were the majority. The caste system continued, and slavery existed. Women's lives varied: elite women (Gulbadan Begum, Nur Jahan, Jahanara) had influence, while most women laboured in fields and households.

Culture: Mughal architecture combined Persian, Central Asian and Indian elements (Humayun's Tomb, Fatehpur Sikri, the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort); painting flourished in the imperial atelier and influenced Rajput and Pahari schools; Persian literature and history-writing (Akbarnama, Ain-i-Akbari, Padshahnama), translations of Sanskrit texts and Hindi devotional poetry (Tulsidas, Surdas) flourished; Hindustani music developed (Tansen); and Urdu emerged as a language.

Religion: Akbar's sulh-i-kul and the Din-i-Ilahi; Jahangir's tolerance alongside the execution of Guru Arjan; Shah Jahan's greater orthodoxy; and Aurangzeb's orthodox policies (reimposition of jizya, temple destruction, execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur) and resulting revolts of the Jats, Satnamis, Sikhs, Rajputs and Marathas. Bhakti and Sufi movements and figures like Dara Shikoh promoted a syncretic culture. Mughal India's distinctive character came from this interaction of diverse traditions.
section-21: Causes of decline: (1) Aurangzeb's long Deccan wars (1681-1707), which exhausted resources and kept the emperor away from the north; (2) his religious policies, which alienated Rajputs, Jats, Sikhs and Marathas (debated); (3) the jagirdari crisis, as the number of mansabdars exceeded available jagirs; (4) weak successors and wars of succession, the rule of the Sayyid brothers as 'king-makers'; (5) factionalism among the nobility; (6) peasant and zamindar revolts against heavy revenue demands (Irfan Habib's agrarian crisis thesis); (7) the rise of regional powers; and (8) foreign invasions by Nadir Shah (1739) and Ahmad Shah Abdali.

Historians' views: Jadunath Sarkar emphasised Aurangzeb's religious bigotry; Satish Chandra the jagirdari crisis; Irfan Habib the exploitation of the peasantry and resulting agrarian revolts; M. Athar Ali the problems of the nobility. Revisionist historians such as Muzaffar Alam and C. A. Bayly argued that the eighteenth century was not a 'dark age' of decline but a period of regional prosperity, when successor states such as Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad grew powerful while still formally recognising the Mughal emperor.

Regional powers: the Marathas (from Shivaji to the Peshwas) expanded across India until defeated at Panipat (1761); the Sikhs organised into misls and later Ranjit Singh's kingdom; the Jats (Suraj Mal of Bharatpur); and successor states of Hyderabad, Bengal and Awadh. The English East India Company took advantage of this situation (Plassey 1757, Buxar 1764). The last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was exiled after 1857, but Mughal culture, administrative practices and court language had lasting influence.
section-22: Warfare: early modern states were built through war. Firearms and artillery, cavalry from the Central Asian tradition, forts, and the 'military labour market' of armed peasants were important. Military success depended on finance (land revenue), alliances and negotiation as much as on battles. In the eighteenth century, European-style infantry and artillery spread among Indian states and the East India Company.

Indian Ocean trade: Indian merchants and ports (Surat, Cambay, Calicut, Masulipatnam, Hooghly) were central to a vast network connecting East Africa, the Middle East, Southeast Asia and China. Textiles were the main export, and silver flowed into India. The arrival of the Portuguese, Dutch, English and French companies gradually changed the structure of trade, but Indian merchants remained important until the late eighteenth century.

South India 1500-1650: Vijayanagara, its Nayaka successors and the Deccan Sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda formed a political economy linking warrior chiefs, temples, agrarian production and long-distance trade. Golconda was famous for diamonds and textiles. Merchant-financiers combined commerce and political roles. Studying these areas shows that early modern India was shaped by multiple centres of power, not only by the Mughal court.
section-25: The Archaic period (c. 800-480 BCE) followed the 'Dark Age' after the collapse of Mycenaean civilisation. It saw the revival of trade, the adoption of the alphabet from the Phoenicians, the composition of Homer's epics, the rise of the polis, colonisation across the Mediterranean and Black Sea, the first Olympic Games (776 BCE), tyrannies and early lawgivers (Draco, Solon).

The Classical period (480-323 BCE) included the Persian Wars, the golden age of Athens under Pericles (the Parthenon, drama of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, philosophy of Socrates and Plato), the Peloponnesian War and the rise of Macedonia. The Hellenistic period (323-31 BCE) began with Alexander's death and lasted until the Roman conquest of Ptolemaic Egypt at Actium.
section-26: Homer's epics (the Iliad and Odyssey) show an early political world of kings (basileis), councils of nobles and assemblies of warriors, and heroic values of honour (time) and excellence (arete). Plato (c. 427-347 BCE), in 'The Republic', sought justice as each class doing its proper work; he proposed rule by philosopher-kings, with guardians and producers, and criticised democracy as rule by the ignorant. He also wrote 'The Laws'.

Aristotle (384-322 BCE), in 'Politics', called man a 'political animal' (zoon politikon) who fulfils himself in the polis. He classified constitutions by the number of rulers and whether they ruled for the common good: monarchy, aristocracy and polity (good forms) and tyranny, oligarchy and democracy (corrupt forms). He favoured a mixed constitution with a strong middle class. Greek thought gave the West concepts such as democracy, citizenship and the rule of law.
section-27: A polis was a self-governing community consisting of a city (often with an acropolis and agora) and its surrounding countryside. There were hundreds of poleis. Athens developed democracy: Solon's reforms (594 BCE), Cleisthenes' reforms (508 BCE, creating ten tribes and the Council of 500) and Pericles' leadership; citizens voted in the Assembly (ekklesia) and served in jury courts, but women, slaves and metics (resident foreigners) were excluded.

Sparta was an oligarchy with two kings, a council of elders (gerousia), five ephors and an assembly; it was a military society in which citizen men (Spartiates) trained from age seven in the agoge, supported by state-owned serfs (helots). Corinth was a wealthy commercial city on the isthmus; Thebes dominated Boeotia and briefly led Greece after defeating Sparta at Leuctra (371 BCE). Delphi (the oracle of Apollo) and Olympia (the Olympic Games, sanctuary of Zeus) were Panhellenic religious centres that united Greeks.
section-28: The Ionian Greek cities of Asia Minor revolted against Persian rule (499 BCE), helped by Athens and Eretria. In response, Darius I invaded Greece, but the Athenians defeated the Persians at Marathon (490 BCE). Xerxes then led a massive invasion (480 BCE): the Spartan king Leonidas and his 300 Spartans died defending the pass of Thermopylae; the Athenian navy, led by Themistocles, won the decisive sea battle at Salamis (480 BCE); and the Greeks won the land battle of Plataea (479 BCE).

Herodotus, the 'father of history', recorded these wars. Results: Greek confidence and identity grew; Athens became the leading naval power and organised the Delian League (478 BCE) against Persia, which turned into an Athenian empire; and the wealth and prestige gained fuelled the Athenian golden age. The wars were seen as a victory of freedom over despotism.
section-29: The Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE) was fought between Athens (with the Delian League, a naval power) and Sparta (with the Peloponnesian League, a land power). Causes, according to the historian Thucydides, were Sparta's fear of growing Athenian power, along with disputes over Corcyra, Potidaea and the Megarian decree. Pericles adopted a strategy of avoiding land battles and relying on the navy, but a plague (430 BCE) killed many Athenians, including Pericles.

After the Peace of Nicias (421 BCE), Athens launched the disastrous Sicilian Expedition (415-413 BCE), promoted by Alcibiades. Persian money helped Sparta build a fleet, and Lysander destroyed the Athenian navy at Aegospotami (405 BCE). Athens surrendered in 404 BCE; the Thirty Tyrants briefly ruled. The war weakened all Greek states, leading to Spartan and Theban dominance and ultimately to the Macedonian conquest.
section-30: The household (oikos) was the basic unit of Greek society, including family members, property and slaves, headed by the male citizen (kyrios). In Athens, women were legal minors under male guardianship, married young (around 14-15) to older men, lived largely within the home (except at festivals and funerals), could not vote or own much property and were valued for producing legitimate heirs. Spartan women had more freedom, owned land and received physical training.

Society was divided into citizens, metics (resident foreigners who paid a special tax and could not own land) and slaves, who were often prisoners of war and performed domestic, agricultural and mining labour (the Laurion silver mines). Athens had perhaps 80,000-100,000 slaves in the fifth century. Aristotle justified 'natural slavery'. Only adult male citizens had full political rights, so Greek democracy was limited.
section-31: Greek natural philosophy began in Ionia: Thales of Miletus (c. 600 BCE) said water was the basic substance and predicted an eclipse; Anaximander and Anaximenes proposed other principles; Pythagoras emphasised numbers and geometry; Democritus proposed that everything consists of atoms. Euclid (geometry, the 'Elements'), Archimedes (the lever, buoyancy), Aristarchus (a sun-centred universe) and Eratosthenes (who measured the earth's circumference) were Hellenistic scientists.

Hippocrates of Cos (c. 460-370 BCE), the 'father of medicine', rejected supernatural explanations of disease and emphasised observation, diet and the balance of four humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile). The Hippocratic Oath still influences medical ethics. Galen (second century CE, in the Roman period) systematised Greek medicine. Aristotle studied biology and classified animals. This rational, observational approach laid foundations for Western science.
section-32: After Alexander's death in 323 BCE, his generals (the Diadochi) divided his empire into kingdoms: the Ptolemies in Egypt (capital Alexandria), the Seleucids in Syria, Mesopotamia and Iran, and the Antigonids in Macedonia; smaller states included Pergamon and Bactria (with Indo-Greek kingdoms later in India). Greek became the common language (koine) of the eastern Mediterranean.

Alexandria became the cultural centre, with its Museum and Library under Ptolemaic patronage, where scholars such as Euclid, Eratosthenes and Herophilus worked. New philosophies included Stoicism (Zeno), emphasising virtue and acceptance of fate, Epicureanism (Epicurus), seeking happiness through moderation and freedom from fear, and Cynicism (Diogenes). Hellenistic art became more realistic and emotional (the Laocoon, Winged Victory of Samothrace). The period ended when Rome conquered the kingdoms, finally Egypt in 31-30 BCE.
section-33: Philip II (r. 359-336 BCE) reorganised the Macedonian army, creating the phalanx with long spears (sarissas) and a powerful cavalry (Companions). Through war, diplomacy and bribery, he gained control of Greece, defeating Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea (338 BCE), despite the warnings of the Athenian orator Demosthenes. He formed the League of Corinth and planned to invade Persia, but was assassinated in 336 BCE.

Alexander III (356-323 BCE), educated by Aristotle, became king at twenty. He crossed into Asia (334 BCE), defeated the Persians at the Granicus, Issus (333 BCE) and Gaugamela (331 BCE), founded Alexandria in Egypt, captured Babylon and Persepolis, and marched to Bactria and India (Hydaspes, 326 BCE). He encouraged a fusion of Greek and Persian cultures (mass marriages at Susa) and founded many cities. He died at Babylon in 323 BCE, aged 32, leaving no strong successor.
section-34: The Etruscans lived in Etruria (modern Tuscany) in central Italy from about the eighth century BCE. They were organised in city-states, were skilled in metalwork and engineering, traded widely and were influenced by Greek culture. Their language is not Indo-European and is only partly understood. Etruscan kings ruled Rome in the sixth century BCE (the Tarquins).

Rome, according to legend, was founded by Romulus in 753 BCE. Etruscan influence on Rome included the arch and drainage engineering (the Cloaca Maxima), the toga, gladiatorial games, divination (haruspicy - reading animal entrails), and the symbols of authority (fasces). In 509 BCE, the Romans overthrew the last Etruscan king, Tarquin the Proud, and established the Republic.
section-35: The Roman Republic (509-27 BCE) was a mixed constitution, as the Greek historian Polybius described it. Two consuls, elected annually, held supreme executive and military power; other magistrates were praetors (justice), quaestors (finance), aediles (public works) and censors (census and morals). A dictator could be appointed for six months in emergencies. The Senate, composed of former magistrates, controlled finance and foreign policy and advised magistrates. Assemblies (comitia centuriata, comitia tributa, concilium plebis) elected magistrates and passed laws.

The 'Struggle of the Orders' between patricians and plebeians led to the creation of tribunes of the plebs (494 BCE), who could veto actions harmful to plebeians, the Twelve Tables (c. 450 BCE), the first written laws, and the Lex Hortensia (287 BCE), which made plebeian assembly decisions binding on all. Rome expanded through conquest and alliances, controlling Italy by 264 BCE.
section-36: The Punic Wars were fought between Rome and Carthage (in modern Tunisia), a Phoenician commercial and naval power. The First Punic War (264-241 BCE) was fought over Sicily; Rome built a navy and won, gaining Sicily, later Sardinia and Corsica. In the Second Punic War (218-201 BCE), Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants and defeated the Romans at Lake Trasimene and Cannae (216 BCE), but could not take Rome. Fabius Maximus avoided battle ('Cunctator'), and Scipio Africanus invaded Africa and defeated Hannibal at Zama (202 BCE).

In the Third Punic War (149-146 BCE), urged by Cato the Elder ('Carthage must be destroyed'), Rome destroyed Carthage completely. The same year, Rome destroyed Corinth and controlled Greece. These victories made Rome the master of the Mediterranean, bringing great wealth, slaves and provinces, but also social problems - the decline of small farmers, the rise of large estates (latifundia) worked by slaves, and political conflict.
section-37: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106-43 BCE) was a lawyer, orator, consul (63 BCE) and philosopher who exposed the Catiline conspiracy. He defended the Republic and the Senate, wrote 'De Re Publica' and 'De Legibus' on the ideal state and natural law, and 'De Officiis' on duties. His speeches against Mark Antony (Philippics) led to his execution. His Latin prose became the model for later centuries.

Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro, 70-19 BCE) wrote the 'Eclogues', 'Georgics' and the epic 'Aeneid', which tells how Aeneas, a Trojan prince, came to Italy and founded the Roman people - glorifying Rome and Augustus. Livy (Titus Livius, 59 BCE-17 CE) wrote 'Ab Urbe Condita' (From the Founding of the City), a history of Rome in 142 books (35 survive), emphasising moral lessons from the past. Both were patronised by Augustus and his minister Maecenas.
section-38: In the late Republic, tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus (133-121 BCE) tried land reforms for the poor and were killed. Marius reformed the army, recruiting landless volunteers who became loyal to their generals. Conflicts between Marius and Sulla, then the Social War with Italian allies, Spartacus' slave revolt (73-71 BCE) and the First Triumvirate (Pompey, Crassus and Julius Caesar, 60 BCE) weakened the Republic.

Caesar conquered Gaul, crossed the Rubicon (49 BCE), defeated Pompey and became dictator for life, but was assassinated on the Ides of March (44 BCE) by Brutus and Cassius. The Second Triumvirate (Octavian, Mark Antony, Lepidus) followed. Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium (31 BCE) and in 27 BCE received the title Augustus, becoming the first emperor while preserving republican forms (the Principate).
section-39: Roman society was hierarchical: senators (senatorial order) and equestrians (knights, wealthy businessmen) at the top; ordinary citizens (plebs); freedmen; and slaves at the bottom. Citizenship was gradually extended, finally to all free inhabitants of the empire by the Constitutio Antoniniana of Caracalla (212 CE). The patron-client relationship tied people of different status together.

The family (familia) was headed by the paterfamilias, who had legal authority (patria potestas) over his wife, children and slaves. Roman women had more freedom than Greek women; elite women could own property and influence politics. Slavery was extensive, with slaves working on latifundia, in mines, households and as gladiators. The army was central to Roman expansion and administration, and roads, aqueducts, law (later codified), Latin, and 'bread and circuses' (free grain and games in the Colosseum) held the empire together. The Pax Romana (27 BCE-180 CE) brought peace and prosperity.
section-40: During the crisis of the third century (235-284 CE), the empire suffered invasions, civil wars, economic decline and plague. Diocletian (284-305) restored order: he created the Tetrarchy (two senior emperors called Augusti and two junior Caesars), divided provinces into smaller units grouped into dioceses, separated civil and military authority, enlarged the army, introduced the Edict of Maximum Prices (301) and persecuted Christians (the 'Great Persecution', 303).

Constantine (306-337) defeated his rival at the Milvian Bridge (312), reportedly after a vision of the Christian symbol, and with Licinius issued the Edict of Milan (313) granting religious toleration. He called the Council of Nicaea (325) and founded Constantinople (330) on the site of Byzantium, which became the capital of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire. Justinian (527-565) reconquered Italy and North Africa, built Hagia Sophia, and compiled the 'Corpus Juris Civilis' (Code of Justinian), which became the basis of European civil law.
section-41: Jesus of Nazareth preached in Roman-ruled Judaea and was crucified around 30-33 CE. His followers, led by Peter and Paul of Tarsus (who preached to non-Jews), spread the faith across the empire, helped by Roman roads, the Greek language and the Pax Romana. Christianity appealed to the poor, slaves and women with its message of salvation, equality before God and charity.

Christians refused to worship the emperor and Roman gods, so they faced persecution, notably under Nero (64 CE), Decius (250) and Diocletian (303). Constantine's Edict of Milan (313) gave toleration, and Theodosius I made Christianity the official state religion (380) and banned pagan worship (391). The church developed bishops, councils (Nicaea 325 produced the Nicene Creed) and the authority of the Bishop of Rome (the Pope). Christianity became the basis of medieval European civilisation.
section-43: Political world: the polis was a self-governing city-state with citizens who took part in government and defence (the hoplite phalanx of citizen soldiers). Athens developed democracy through Solon, Cleisthenes and Pericles, with an Assembly of all male citizens, a Council of 500 chosen by lot and popular courts; ostracism exiled dangerous politicians. Sparta was a military oligarchy based on helot labour and the agoge. Common culture united Greeks through religion (Olympian gods, Delphi), the Olympic Games, language and Homer.

Political thought: Homer's heroic values; the Sophists, who taught rhetoric and questioned traditional values; Socrates (executed in 399 BCE), who questioned everything through dialogue; Plato's ideal state ruled by philosopher-kings; and Aristotle's classification of constitutions and preference for a mixed constitution. Wars: the Persian Wars (Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, Plataea) united the Greeks against Persia and raised Athens to leadership; the Delian League became the Athenian empire; the Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE) destroyed Athenian power and weakened Greece.

Society and science: the oikos was headed by men; women were secluded in Athens but freer in Sparta; slaves and metics lacked political rights. Greek science (Thales, Pythagoras, Democritus) and medicine (Hippocrates) sought natural explanations; history-writing began with Herodotus and Thucydides; drama (Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, Aristophanes) and architecture (the Parthenon) reached great heights. Greek civilisation laid the foundations of Western philosophy, politics and science.
section-44: Rise of Macedonia: Philip II created a professional army with the sarissa-armed phalanx and Companion cavalry, expanded through war and diplomacy, and defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea (338 BCE). He established the League of Corinth under Macedonian leadership. Alexander inherited this army and the plan to invade Persia.

Alexander's conquests: Granicus (334), Issus (333), Tyre and Egypt (332, founding Alexandria), Gaugamela (331), Persepolis (330), Bactria and Sogdiana, and India (Hydaspes against Porus, 326). His army's refusal at the Beas forced his return; he died at Babylon in 323 BCE. He adopted Persian dress and court ceremonial, married Roxane and encouraged Macedonian-Persian marriages, which some see as a policy of fusion of cultures.

Hellenistic world: the Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Antigonid kingdoms spread Greek language and institutions across the Near East. Alexandria's Library and Museum promoted science (Euclid, Archimedes, Eratosthenes) and scholarship; philosophy turned to individual happiness (Stoicism, Epicureanism); art became realistic and emotional; and Greek and local religions mingled (Serapis cult in Egypt). In Bactria and India, Indo-Greek kingdoms influenced coinage and Gandhara art. Rome absorbed the Hellenistic world by 30 BCE but adopted much of its culture.
section-45: Early Rome: according to tradition founded in 753 BCE, Rome was ruled by kings, the last three of whom were Etruscan. Etruscan influence included engineering, religious practices, symbols of authority and urban planning. The Republic was established in 509 BCE.

Republican institutions: the consuls, praetors, quaestors, aediles, censors and tribunes; the Senate; and the assemblies. The patrician-plebeian conflict produced the tribunes, the Twelve Tables and the Lex Hortensia. Roman expansion in Italy used alliances, colonies and roads (the Via Appia). The Punic Wars against Carthage - First (Sicily), Second (Hannibal, Cannae, Zama) and Third (destruction of Carthage, 146 BCE) - and wars in Greece and the East made Rome a Mediterranean empire. Expansion brought wealth, slaves, provinces governed by Roman governors and the rise of large estates, causing social tension.

Writers: Cicero, the great orator and defender of the Republic, wrote on law and the state; Virgil's Aeneid gave Rome a national epic linking it to Troy and glorifying Augustus; Livy's history celebrated Roman virtues of courage, discipline and piety. These writers shaped Latin literature and Western ideas of law, government and history.
section-46: From Republic to Empire: the Gracchi's reforms, the army reforms of Marius, the civil wars of Marius and Sulla, the First Triumvirate, Caesar's dictatorship and assassination, and the Second Triumvirate destroyed the Republic. Augustus (27 BCE-14 CE) established the Principate, keeping republican forms but holding real power. The Pax Romana followed, with emperors such as Trajan (who expanded the empire to its greatest extent), Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius.

Society and crisis: Roman society included senators, equestrians, citizens, freedmen and slaves; the paterfamilias headed the family; citizenship spread (212 CE); law, roads, aqueducts and cities unified the empire. The third-century crisis brought invasions, civil wars and inflation. Diocletian's reforms (Tetrarchy, administrative and economic reforms) and Constantine's (Christian toleration, Constantinople, the gold solidus) restored the empire temporarily. The Western Empire fell in 476 CE when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus; the Eastern Empire continued until 1453, with Justinian's legal code and Hagia Sophia as its great achievements.

Christianity: from its origins in Judaea, it spread through Paul and the apostles, faced persecution, won toleration (313) and became the state religion (380). The church adopted Roman administrative structures (dioceses), Latin and Greek, and became the main institution preserving learning after the fall of the Western Empire. Rome thus left legacies in law, language, architecture, government and religion.
section-49: Sex refers to biological differences (chromosomes, reproductive organs), while gender refers to the social and cultural meanings, roles and behaviour associated with being male or female. Simone de Beauvoir's statement 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' (1949) is a classic expression of social construction. Ann Oakley ('Sex, Gender and Society', 1972) popularised the distinction in social science.

Gender roles vary across societies and periods, showing they are not natural. For example, weaving and agriculture were women's work in some societies and men's in others. Judith Butler later argued that even ideas of sex are shaped by culture and that gender is 'performative'. Gender history studies how such roles are created and change over time and how they relate to power.
section-50: Patriarchy literally means 'rule of the father'. Gerda Lerner's 'The Creation of Patriarchy' (1986) traced its historical development in ancient Mesopotamia, arguing that it was a historical creation, not natural, and could therefore be ended. Kate Millett ('Sexual Politics', 1970) saw it as the most pervasive ideology of society. Sylvia Walby identified structures of patriarchy in household production, paid work, the state, violence, sexuality and culture.

In India, historians such as Uma Chakravarti ('Gendering Caste', 2003) have shown how 'Brahmanical patriarchy' combined caste and gender control - controlling women's sexuality to maintain caste purity. Patriarchy differs by class, caste, religion and region, and it interacts with other forms of inequality.
section-51: Feminism is both a theory and a movement for women's equality. Mary Wollstonecraft's 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman' (1792) is an early classic. Types of feminism include liberal feminism (equal legal rights and opportunities, e.g. John Stuart Mill's 'The Subjection of Women', 1869), radical feminism (patriarchy as the root of oppression), Marxist and socialist feminism (linking women's oppression to capitalism and class), black feminism (bell hooks, Audre Lorde) and postcolonial feminism (Chandra Talpade Mohanty's critique of Western feminism's image of 'Third World women').

Feminist history has challenged historians to include women and gender in their research, question 'universal' narratives that were really about men, and examine everyday life and family as sites of power.
section-52: Traditional history focused on politics, war, kings and great men - areas from which women were mostly excluded - and used sources produced by men. From the 1960s-1970s, influenced by the second-wave women's movement and social history ('history from below'), historians began to recover women's lives - their work, family roles, sexuality, religion, protests and contributions.

Pioneers include Gerda Lerner (USA), Sheila Rowbotham ('Hidden from History', 1973), Natalie Zemon Davis and Joan Kelly, whose essay 'Did Women Have a Renaissance?' (1977) showed that periods celebrated as progressive might not have been so for women. In India, works such as Kumkum Sangari and Sudesh Vaid's 'Recasting Women' (1989), Tanika Sarkar and Geraldine Forbes ('Women in Modern India') are important.
section-53: Women's history is significant because it makes history complete - half of humanity was missing from historical writing. It reveals new topics: domestic work, childbirth and motherhood, sexuality, women's labour in fields and factories, women's religious and cultural roles and their participation in movements such as the Indian freedom struggle.

It also changes our understanding of familiar events and periods (for example, how colonialism or industrialisation affected women differently), questions the division between 'public' and 'private' spheres, and uses new sources such as oral history, diaries, letters, songs and court records. It empowers women by showing their agency in the past and helps explain present inequalities.
section-54: Approaches include: (1) 'compensatory' or 'contribution' history, which adds notable women (queens, reformers, writers) to existing narratives; (2) the oppression approach, which studies how patriarchy subordinated women through law, religion, family and work; (3) the agency approach, which shows how women resisted, negotiated and shaped their lives within constraints; (4) social history of women's everyday lives, labour and family; and (5) Marxist-feminist approaches linking gender and class.

Later approaches emphasise difference - women's experiences differ by class, caste, race, religion, region and sexuality - and intersectionality. Postcolonial approaches warn against seeing non-Western women only as victims. Gender history (from the 1980s) moved beyond studying only women to studying the relations between men and women and the construction of masculinity.
section-55: Joan Wallach Scott's essay 'Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis' (1986) is the key text. She defined gender as 'a constitutive element of social relationships based on perceived differences between the sexes' and 'a primary way of signifying relationships of power'. Gender operates through cultural symbols, normative concepts (religious, legal and scientific doctrines), social institutions (family, labour market, education, polity) and subjective identity.

This means historians can use gender to analyse politics, war, nationalism, colonialism and class even where women are absent - for example, how colonial rulers described Indians as 'effeminate' to justify rule, or how nationalism used the image of 'Mother India'. Studying masculinity (how manhood is constructed) is part of this approach. Gender thus becomes a tool for understanding all of society.
section-56: First-wave feminism (mid-nineteenth to early twentieth century) emerged in Britain and the USA. The Seneca Falls Convention (1848) in New York, led by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott, adopted the 'Declaration of Sentiments' demanding equal rights including the vote. Susan B. Anthony was a leading campaigner. In Britain, Millicent Fawcett led the suffragists (constitutional methods), and Emmeline Pankhurst's Women's Social and Political Union (1903) - the suffragettes - used militant tactics.

Demands included the right to vote, property rights for married women, access to education and professions and reform of divorce and custody laws. New Zealand gave women the vote in 1893; Britain in 1918 (partially) and 1928 (equally); the USA in 1920 (Nineteenth Amendment). First-wave feminism was largely led by middle-class white women and focused on legal equality.
section-57: Second-wave feminism (1960s-1980s) began with books such as Simone de Beauvoir's 'The Second Sex' (1949) and Betty Friedan's 'The Feminine Mystique' (1963), which described the dissatisfaction of educated American housewives ('the problem that has no name'). The National Organization for Women (NOW) was founded in 1966. Its slogan 'the personal is political' (Carol Hanisch) meant that private issues - housework, sexuality, violence - were political matters.

Issues included equal pay (the Equal Pay Act, 1963 in the USA; 1970 in the UK), workplace discrimination, reproductive rights (the US Supreme Court decision in Roe v. Wade, 1973), domestic violence, rape, sexual freedom and the representation of women in media. Radical feminists (Shulamith Firestone, Kate Millett) analysed patriarchy as a system. Critics noted that second-wave feminism often ignored the different concerns of women of colour, working-class women and lesbians.
section-58: Third-wave feminism (from the early 1990s) was named by Rebecca Walker in 1992. It responded to criticisms of second-wave feminism by emphasising diversity, individuality and the different experiences of women by race, class, sexuality, nationality and religion. Kimberlé Crenshaw's concept of intersectionality (1989) explained how different forms of discrimination overlap.

It drew on postmodern and post-structuralist theories (Judith Butler's 'Gender Trouble', 1990), queer theory and postcolonial feminism. It embraced popular culture, reclaimed words and styles previously seen as anti-feminist (the 'Riot Grrrl' movement), and focused on issues such as sexual harassment (the Anita Hill hearings, 1991), global women's rights and identity. A fourth wave (from about 2012) uses social media, for example the #MeToo movement (2017).
section-59: Nineteenth-century social reformers focused on the 'women's question': Raja Rammohun Roy campaigned against sati, which Lord William Bentinck banned in 1829; Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar promoted widow remarriage (Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856) and girls' education; the Brahmo Samaj, Prarthana Samaj and Arya Samaj promoted reform; Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a girls' school in Pune (1848); and B. M. Malabari's campaign led to the Age of Consent Act (1891), raising the age of consent from 10 to 12.

Women themselves began to speak: Pandita Ramabai (who founded Sharada Sadan for widows and wrote 'The High-Caste Hindu Woman', 1887), Tarabai Shinde ('Stri Purush Tulana', 1882, comparing men and women), Rassundari Devi (the first autobiography in Bengali, 'Amar Jiban', 1876), Anandibai Joshi and Kadambini Ganguly (the first women doctors), Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain ('Sultana's Dream', 1905). Historians note that early reforms were often led by men and aimed at creating 'modern' wives and mothers within a patriarchal framework.
section-60: Women's organisations formed: the Women's Indian Association (1917, Annie Besant, Margaret Cousins), the National Council of Women in India (1925) and the All India Women's Conference (AIWC, 1927), which campaigned for education, the Sarda Act (Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1929) and legal reform. Sarojini Naidu led a delegation for women's franchise in 1917 and became Congress President in 1925.

Gandhi brought large numbers of women into the national movement: in the Non-Cooperation movement, picketing liquor and foreign cloth shops; in the Salt Satyagraha (1930), when thousands were arrested; and in the Quit India movement (1942), when Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag and Usha Mehta ran a secret radio. Revolutionary women included Pritilata Waddedar and Kalpana Dutta (Chittagong), and Captain Lakshmi Sehgal led the INA's Rani of Jhansi Regiment. The Karachi resolution (1931) promised equal rights for women. Women's participation was significant, though their roles were often seen as an extension of domestic virtues.
section-61: The Constitution (1950) guaranteed equality (Articles 14, 15 and 16) and universal adult franchise. The Hindu Code Bills (1955-1956) - the Hindu Marriage Act, Hindu Succession Act and others, championed by B. R. Ambedkar - gave Hindu women rights of divorce and inheritance. The 'Towards Equality' report (1974) of the Committee on the Status of Women showed declining sex ratios and continuing inequality, sparking a new women's movement.

From the late 1970s, movements arose against dowry deaths, rape (the Mathura case, 1979, led to amendments in 1983), sati (Roop Kanwar, 1987) and domestic violence. Laws include the Dowry Prohibition Act (1961), the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act (2005), the Vishaka guidelines (1997) and the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act (2013), and criminal law amendments after the 2012 Delhi gang rape. The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) reserved one-third of seats for women in local bodies; the Women's Reservation Act (2023) provides for one-third reservation in Parliament and state assemblies. Dalit, tribal and Muslim women's movements have highlighted differences among women.
section-63: Sex and gender: biology does not determine social roles; gender is socially constructed and varies across time and place. Gender history asks how societies defined what was 'appropriate' for men and women, how these definitions were enforced through family, religion, law, education and economy, and how they changed. Masculinity is also constructed - ideas of manliness shaped warfare, politics and work.

Patriarchy: a system of male dominance found in most historical societies, but in varying forms. Gerda Lerner showed it was historically created. In India, Brahmanical patriarchy linked caste purity with control of women's sexuality (Uma Chakravarti). Feminism: theories and movements - liberal, radical, Marxist, socialist, black and postcolonial - that challenge gender inequality in different ways.

Why gender history matters: it reveals hidden experiences; it changes periodisation (as Joan Kelly asked whether women had a Renaissance); it shows how gender relates to class, caste, race and colonialism; and it exposes how power operates in everyday life. As Joan Scott argued, gender is a primary way of signifying power, so it is relevant to every area of history, including politics and war.
section-64: Women's history: emerged in the 1960s-1970s from the women's movement and social history. It recovered women's experiences through new sources and methods (oral history, diaries, songs, court records). Historians such as Sheila Rowbotham, Gerda Lerner and Natalie Zemon Davis, and in India Geraldine Forbes, Uma Chakravarti and Tanika Sarkar, made important contributions.

Approaches: contribution history (adding famous women), oppression history (structures of subordination), agency history (women's resistance and initiative), social history (everyday life, work and family) and Marxist-feminist analysis (gender and class). Later approaches emphasised difference and intersectionality and criticised treating 'women' as a single group. Each approach has strengths - recovering experiences, explaining structures - and weaknesses, such as treating women only as victims or ignoring differences.

Gender as an analytical category: Joan Scott (1986) argued that gender should be used to analyse all aspects of society - symbols, norms, institutions and identities - and that gender is a way of signifying power. For example, colonial discourse described Bengali men as effeminate, nationalists portrayed the nation as a mother, and debates about sati were really debates about tradition and colonial authority (Lata Mani). Gender history thus moves from 'adding women' to rethinking history as a whole.
section-65: First wave (c. 1848-1920): Seneca Falls Convention (1848); the suffrage campaigns in the USA (Stanton, Anthony) and Britain (Fawcett's suffragists, Pankhurst's suffragettes); demands for the vote, property rights, education and legal personhood. Women won the vote in New Zealand (1893), Britain (1918/1928) and the USA (1920). The movement was mostly middle-class and white.

Second wave (c. 1960s-1980s): de Beauvoir and Friedan inspired a broad movement; 'the personal is political'; campaigns for equal pay, anti-discrimination laws, reproductive rights, against violence and for sexual freedom; radical feminist analysis of patriarchy; consciousness-raising groups. It was criticised for focusing on the concerns of white, middle-class Western women.

Third wave (from the 1990s): diversity, intersectionality (Crenshaw), queer theory (Butler), global and postcolonial perspectives, individual identity and popular culture. A fourth wave uses digital activism (#MeToo). Critique of the 'wave' model: it suggests periods of silence between waves, centres Western history and hides diversity within each period; feminist activity was continuous and global. Still, the wave model is a helpful way to understand changing priorities.
section-66: First phase (1850-1915): social reform movements led mainly by men - against sati (1829), for widow remarriage (1856), education of girls and raising the age of consent (1891). Reformers included Rammohun Roy, Vidyasagar, Phule, Ranade and Malabari. Women such as Pandita Ramabai, Tarabai Shinde, Savitribai Phule and Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain began to articulate their own views. Historians (Partha Chatterjee) argue that nationalists 'resolved' the women's question by placing women in an inner, spiritual domain as guardians of Indian tradition.

Second phase (1915-1947): women's organisations (WIA 1917, AIWC 1927) campaigned for franchise and legal reform (the Sarda Act, 1929); mass participation in Gandhian movements (Non-Cooperation, Salt Satyagraha, Quit India); revolutionary women (Pritilata Waddedar, Bina Das) and the INA's Rani of Jhansi Regiment; the Karachi resolution's promise of equal rights. Women entered public life in large numbers, but the national movement often subordinated gender questions to the national cause.

Third phase (1947-present): constitutional equality; the Hindu Code Bills; the 'Towards Equality' report (1974) and the autonomous women's movement against dowry, rape, sati and violence; legal reforms; reservations in local bodies (1992) and legislatures (2023 Act); and movements of Dalit, tribal and Muslim women. 'Doing gender' in India means examining how gender intersects with caste, class, religion and region in specific historical conditions.
section-69: Causes: political - Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse (annexing Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur), the annexation of Awadh (1856) on grounds of misgovernment, and disrespect towards the Mughal emperor; economic - heavy land revenue, the ruin of artisans and loss of zamindars' estates; social and religious - fear of conversion, laws such as the Widow Remarriage Act and missionary activity; military - low pay, discrimination, the General Service Enlistment Act (1856) requiring overseas service, and the immediate cause, the greased cartridges of the Enfield rifle rumoured to contain cow and pig fat.

The revolt began at Meerut on 10 May 1857 (after Mangal Pandey's earlier act at Barrackpore in March); sepoys marched to Delhi and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar emperor. Leaders included Nana Saheb and Tantia Tope (Kanpur), Begum Hazrat Mahal (Lucknow), Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi), Kunwar Singh (Bihar) and Maulvi Ahmadullah (Faizabad). It was suppressed by 1858. Consequences: the Government of India Act 1858 ended Company rule; Queen Victoria's Proclamation promised non-interference in religion and an end to annexation; the army was reorganised. V. D. Savarkar called it the 'First War of Indian Independence'; others call it a sepoy mutiny or a popular revolt.
section-70: The Indian National Congress was founded in December 1885 at Bombay, with A. O. Hume's help and W. C. Bonnerjee as the first president. Moderate leaders (1885-1905) included Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjea, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Badruddin Tyabji and M. G. Ranade. They believed in British justice and used 'prayer, petition and protest' through resolutions, speeches and delegations.

Demands: expansion of legislative councils, Indianisation of the civil services (simultaneous ICS examinations in India), reduction of military expenditure and land revenue, separation of judiciary and executive, and protection of civil rights. Their economic critique - especially Naoroji's 'Drain of Wealth' theory - exposed colonial exploitation. Achievements: the Indian Councils Act (1892), political education, and building national unity. Limitations: a narrow social base among the educated elite and limited success.
section-71: The Extremists or 'Assertive Nationalists' - Bal Gangadhar Tilak ('Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it'), Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal (Lal-Bal-Pal), and Aurobindo Ghosh - criticised the moderates' 'political mendicancy'. They demanded swaraj (self-rule), believed in self-reliance and mass action, and drew on India's cultural heritage (Tilak's Ganapati and Shivaji festivals) to mobilise people.

Their methods were swadeshi (use of Indian goods), boycott of British goods and institutions, national education and passive resistance. The split between moderates and extremists occurred at the Surat session (1907). The government repressed the extremists - Tilak was imprisoned in Mandalay (1908-1914). Factors behind their rise included the failure of moderate methods, Curzon's policies (especially the partition of Bengal), famine and plague, and international events such as Japan's victory over Russia (1905).
section-72: Lord Curzon announced the partition of Bengal in July 1905; it came into effect on 16 October 1905. Bengal was divided into West Bengal (with Bihar and Odisha) and Eastern Bengal and Assam, with Dacca as capital. The official reason was administrative convenience, since the province was very large (78 million people), but nationalists saw it as an attempt to weaken Bengali nationalism and divide Hindus and Muslims, since the east had a Muslim majority. Curzon's officials said privately that 'Bengal united is a power; Bengal divided will pull in different ways'.

16 October 1905 was observed as a day of mourning; Rabindranath Tagore composed 'Amar Sonar Bangla' and people tied rakhis as a sign of unity. The partition sparked the Swadeshi movement. It was annulled in 1911 at the Delhi Durbar of King George V, when the capital was moved from Calcutta to Delhi. However, the partition encouraged the formation of the Muslim League (1906).
section-73: The Swadeshi movement was formally proclaimed at a meeting in the Calcutta Town Hall on 7 August 1905. It promoted Indian-made goods and the boycott of British goods, especially Manchester cloth and Liverpool salt, through bonfires of foreign cloth and picketing of shops. Indian enterprises grew: textile mills, soap and match factories, the Bengal Chemicals of P. C. Ray and swadeshi banks and insurance companies. V. O. Chidambaram Pillai started the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company at Tuticorin.

National education: the National Council of Education (1906) and Bengal National College (with Aurobindo as principal). Samitis (volunteer organisations) such as Ashwini Kumar Dutta's Swadesh Bandhab Samiti mobilised people. Culture flourished - Tagore's songs, Abanindranath Tagore's art. The movement spread beyond Bengal (Tilak in Maharashtra, Lajpat Rai in Punjab, Chidambaram Pillai in Madras). It declined after 1908 due to repression, the Surat split and limited mass participation, especially among Muslim peasants, but it was a major step towards mass nationalism.
section-74: During the First World War, two Home Rule Leagues were founded on the model of the Irish Home Rule movement: Tilak's league (April 1916, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Central Provinces and Berar) and Annie Besant's All India Home Rule League (September 1916, rest of India). They demanded self-government within the British Empire through lectures, newspapers (Besant's 'New India' and 'Commonweal'), discussion groups and pamphlets.

The movement revived nationalist activity after a period of inactivity, brought new people (Jawaharlal Nehru, Mohammed Ali Jinnah, Chittaranjan Das and others) into politics, and spread to new areas. Besant's internment in 1917 led to protests. The movement contributed to the Lucknow Pact (1916) between Congress and the Muslim League and to the reunion of moderates and extremists, and influenced the Montagu Declaration (August 1917) promising 'responsible government'. It declined after 1918 as Gandhi emerged.
section-75: The All India Muslim League was founded at Dacca on 30 December 1906, led by the Aga Khan and Nawab Salimullah of Dacca, after a deputation (the Simla Deputation, October 1906) asked Lord Minto for separate electorates. The Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) granted separate electorates for Muslims. The League initially supported British rule, then cooperated with Congress (Lucknow Pact, 1916). Under Jinnah, it adopted the Lahore Resolution (23 March 1940), demanding separate states for Muslims (Pakistan), based on the 'two-nation theory'.

The Hindu Mahasabha was formed (as an all-India body from 1915) by leaders such as Madan Mohan Malaviya, later led by V. D. Savarkar ('Hindutva', 1923), and promoted Hindu interests and Hindu nationalism. The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) was founded in 1925 by K. B. Hedgewar. Communalism - the belief that religious communities have separate political and economic interests - grew due to British policies (divide and rule, separate electorates), the economic competition of the middle classes, and communal riots. It eventually contributed to Partition.
section-76: The Communist Party of India was founded in 1920 at Tashkent by M. N. Roy and others (a group in India formally organised it at Kanpur in 1925). Communists were prosecuted in the Peshawar, Kanpur (1924) and Meerut Conspiracy Cases (1929-1933). They organised trade unions (AITUC, 1920, with its first president Lala Lajpat Rai) and peasant organisations (All India Kisan Sabha, 1936). They opposed the Quit India Movement in 1942 because of the 'People's War' line after the Soviet Union joined the Allies.

The Congress Socialist Party (CSP) was founded in 1934 within Congress by Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev, Ram Manohar Lohia, Minoo Masani and Achyut Patwardhan, to give the national movement a socialist direction. Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose were sympathetic to socialism. The left pushed Congress to adopt pro-peasant and pro-worker programmes (the Karachi resolution of 1931 on Fundamental Rights and Economic Policy, and the Faizpur agrarian programme of 1936).
section-77: Bhagat Singh (1907-1931), from Punjab, was influenced by the Ghadar movement, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919) and socialist ideas. With Chandrashekhar Azad, Sukhdev and others, he reorganised the Hindustan Republican Association as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA, 1928), aiming for a socialist republic. To avenge Lala Lajpat Rai's death after a police lathi-charge during the Simon Commission protest, he and Rajguru killed police officer J. P. Saunders (1928).

On 8 April 1929, Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw harmless bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly, shouting 'Inquilab Zindabad', and allowed themselves to be arrested, to use the trial for propaganda ('to make the deaf hear'). In jail he went on hunger strike and wrote 'Why I am an Atheist'. He, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged on 23 March 1931 in Lahore. He became a symbol of revolutionary courage and socialist ideals.
section-78: Surya Sen ('Masterda'), a schoolteacher, led the Indian Republican Army in Chittagong (now in Bangladesh). On 18 April 1930, his group raided the police and auxiliary force armouries in Chittagong, cut telegraph and railway lines and proclaimed a provisional revolutionary government. Many young men and women took part, including Ganesh Ghosh, Ananta Singh, Lokenath Bal and Kalpana Dutta.

After a battle at Jalalabad hills, where several revolutionaries were killed, the group continued guerrilla attacks. Pritilata Waddedar led an attack on the Pahartali European Club (1932) and took poison to avoid capture. Surya Sen was arrested in 1933 and hanged in January 1934. The raid showed the participation of women in revolutionary activity and inspired later generations.
section-79: The INA (Azad Hind Fauj) was first formed in 1942 by Captain Mohan Singh, with Indian prisoners of war captured by Japan in Malaya and Singapore, with support from Rash Behari Bose's Indian Independence League. Subhas Chandra Bose, who had escaped from house arrest in 1941 and gone to Germany, arrived in Singapore in 1943 and took command. He formed the Provisional Government of Free India (Azad Hind) on 21 October 1943, gave the slogans 'Delhi Chalo' and 'Give me blood, and I will give you freedom', and created the Rani of Jhansi Regiment under Captain Lakshmi Swaminathan (Sehgal).

The INA fought alongside the Japanese in the Imphal and Kohima campaigns (1944) in Manipur and Nagaland, but was defeated; Bose reportedly died in an air crash in Taiwan in August 1945. The British trial of INA officers (Shah Nawaz Khan, P. K. Sahgal and G. S. Dhillon) at the Red Fort (1945-1946) caused nationwide protests and showed that the loyalty of the Indian armed forces could no longer be relied upon, which hastened independence.
section-80: On 18 February 1946, ratings (sailors) of the Royal Indian Navy on HMIS Talwar in Bombay went on strike against racial discrimination, poor food, low pay and the INA trials. The mutiny spread to about 78 ships and 20 shore establishments in Bombay, Karachi, Calcutta, Madras and elsewhere, involving about 20,000 ratings. The mutineers raised Congress, Muslim League and Communist flags together, and workers in Bombay struck in support.

The British used force; Congress leaders (Vallabhbhai Patel) and Jinnah persuaded the ratings to surrender on 23 February, as they feared indiscipline and violence. The mutiny showed the decline of British control over the armed forces and contributed to Britain's decision to send the Cabinet Mission and leave India.
section-81: Gandhi (1869-1948) developed satyagraha (truth-force, non-violent resistance) in South Africa (1893-1914) against racial discrimination. In India, he led local struggles in Champaran (1917, indigo farmers), Ahmedabad (1918, mill workers' strike) and Kheda (1918, peasants' revenue remission). He opposed the Rowlatt Act (1919) with a nationwide hartal; the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) followed.

His methods - non-violence, non-cooperation, civil disobedience, fasting, constructive work (khadi, Hindu-Muslim unity, removal of untouchability, village industries) - and his simple lifestyle and use of religious symbols and Indian languages brought peasants, women, workers and ordinary people into the movement, transforming the Congress into a mass organisation. Historians debate his relationship with peasant radicalism and his compromises, but his role in creating a mass, non-violent national movement is undisputed.
section-82: Causes: the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh massacre, the inadequate Montagu-Chelmsford reforms (1919), the Hunter Committee's whitewash, and the Khilafat issue (Muslim anger at the treatment of the Ottoman Caliph after the First World War). Gandhi joined the Khilafat leaders (the Ali brothers) and the Congress adopted the programme at Calcutta (September 1920) and Nagpur (December 1920).

Programme: surrender of titles, boycott of legislatures, law courts, government schools and colleges, and foreign cloth; promotion of swadeshi, khadi, national schools (Jamia Millia Islamia, Kashi Vidyapith), and panchayats; and possibly non-payment of taxes. There were strikes, peasant movements (Awadh, Malabar - the Mappila rebellion) and tribal movements. Gandhi promised 'swaraj within a year'. After a mob burned a police station at Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur) on 5 February 1922, killing 22 policemen, Gandhi called off the movement. It made Congress a mass party and spread nationalism to villages.
section-83: Background: the Simon Commission boycott (1928), the Nehru Report, and the Lahore Congress (December 1929) under Jawaharlal Nehru, which declared Purna Swaraj (complete independence) as the goal; 26 January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day. Gandhi's eleven demands to the Viceroy were rejected. On 12 March 1930, he began the Dandi March from Sabarmati Ashram with 78 followers, walking 240 miles to Dandi, where he broke the salt law on 6 April 1930.

The movement spread: salt was made illegally, foreign cloth and liquor were boycotted, forest laws were broken, and taxes were refused. Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan's Khudai Khidmatgars (Red Shirts) in the North-West Frontier, Rani Gaidinliu in Nagaland and Manipur, and C. Rajagopalachari's salt march in Tamil Nadu (Vedaranyam) were notable; over 90,000 were arrested. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931) suspended it; Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference, which failed. The movement was resumed (1932) and withdrawn in 1934. It involved more women and a wider social base than Non-Cooperation.
section-84: After the failure of the Cripps Mission, the threat of Japanese invasion and growing discontent, the Congress passed the Quit India resolution at Bombay on 8 August 1942. Gandhi gave the call 'Do or Die'. The next morning, Gandhi and all major leaders were arrested.

The leaderless movement saw spontaneous protests, strikes, attacks on railway lines, police stations and government buildings, and the formation of parallel governments in Ballia (Uttar Pradesh), Tamluk (Bengal, Jatiya Sarkar) and Satara (Maharashtra, Prati Sarkar). Underground leaders included Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia, Aruna Asaf Ali and Usha Mehta (Congress Radio). The government crushed it with great force - over 100,000 arrests and about 1,000 deaths officially. The Muslim League and Communists did not support it. The movement showed the depth of nationalist feeling and made clear that British rule could not continue for long after the war.
section-85: The Simon Commission (1927), appointed under the Government of India Act 1919 to review constitutional progress, had seven British members and no Indians. It was boycotted with black flags and the slogan 'Simon Go Back' when it arrived in 1928; Lala Lajpat Rai was injured in a lathi-charge in Lahore and died. Secretary of State Lord Birkenhead challenged Indians to produce an agreed constitution.

An All Parties Conference appointed a committee chaired by Motilal Nehru, which produced the Nehru Report (August 1928). It proposed dominion status, a federal structure, responsible government, a list of fundamental rights, universal adult franchise, joint electorates with reserved seats for minorities and linguistic provinces. Jinnah's 'Fourteen Points' (1929) rejected it, and young radicals (Jawaharlal Nehru, Subhas Bose) wanted complete independence. The Lahore Congress (1929) then adopted Purna Swaraj.
section-86: In March 1942, with Japan advancing in Southeast Asia and under pressure from the USA and China, the British government sent Sir Stafford Cripps to India. His proposals: dominion status after the war; a constituent assembly elected by provincial legislatures and nominated by princes; the right of any province to stay out of the new union (opting out); and Indian participation in the war-time government, but with defence under British control.

The Congress rejected the offer because it promised only dominion status in the future, gave no real power immediately and the opt-out clause opened the way to partition; Gandhi reportedly called it a 'post-dated cheque on a crashing bank'. The Muslim League rejected it because it did not explicitly accept Pakistan. The failure led to the Quit India Movement.
section-87: The Wavell Plan (June 1945), proposed by Viceroy Lord Wavell, offered to reconstitute the Executive Council with all members Indian except the Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief, with equal representation of caste Hindus and Muslims. At the Simla Conference, Jinnah insisted that the League alone should nominate all Muslim members, which the Congress (whose president was Maulana Azad, a Muslim) refused, so the conference failed.

The Cabinet Mission (March-June 1946) - Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A. V. Alexander - proposed a federal union with control over defence, foreign affairs and communications; provinces grouped into three sections (Group A Hindu-majority, Groups B and C in the north-west and east with Muslim majorities); a Constituent Assembly; and an interim government. The League accepted at first, then withdrew after a dispute over the grouping and called for 'Direct Action Day' (16 August 1946), which led to the Calcutta riots. The interim government under Nehru was formed in September 1946, and the League later joined it.
section-88: In February 1947, British Prime Minister Clement Attlee announced that Britain would leave India by June 1948. Lord Mountbatten became Viceroy in March 1947. Finding the situation deteriorating with communal riots, he announced the 3 June Plan (Mountbatten Plan): India would be partitioned into two dominions, India and Pakistan; the legislative assemblies of Punjab and Bengal would vote on partition of their provinces; a referendum would be held in the North-West Frontier Province and Sylhet; and princely states could join either dominion or remain independent.

The date of transfer was advanced to 15 August 1947. Boundary commissions under Sir Cyril Radcliffe drew the borders in Punjab and Bengal. Partition caused massive violence and the migration of about 10-15 million people, with perhaps up to a million deaths. Congress and the League accepted the plan as the only way to end the deadlock.
section-89: The Indian Independence Act was passed by the British Parliament on 18 July 1947 based on the Mountbatten Plan. Its provisions: two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, from 15 August 1947; the end of British paramountcy over princely states; the Constituent Assemblies of each dominion would have full legislative power and could frame their constitutions; the British Crown would no longer be responsible for government; the office of Secretary of State for India was abolished; and each dominion would have a Governor-General.

Mountbatten became the first Governor-General of India and Jinnah of Pakistan. The princely states were integrated into India largely through the efforts of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V. P. Menon using the Instrument of Accession, though Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir posed problems. The Act ended British rule after nearly two centuries.
